note: Illustrative negotiation playbook for a mid-market SaaS buyer. Positions are generic commercial norms, not legal advice; a real deployment loads the company's own playbook here.

entries.definition: A limitation of liability clause caps the damages one party can recover from the other, usually to fees paid over a trailing period, and carves out categories such as indemnity, confidentiality breach and gross negligence.
entries.standard_position: Mutual cap at 12 months of fees paid; uncapped for indemnification obligations, breach of confidentiality, gross negligence and wilful misconduct; consequential damages waiver mutual.
fallbacks: Cap at the greater of 12 months of fees or a fixed floor amount
Super-cap of 2x annual fees for data-breach claims
Accept vendor cap if it is at least 12 months of fees and carve-outs survive

precedents.text: Vendor proposed a $5,000 aggregate cap against a $240,000 annual contract. Rejected; settled at 12 months of fees with data-breach super-cap of 24 months.
Vendor asked for a one-way cap (vendor capped, customer uncapped). Countered with mutual cap; accepted.

entries.definition: An indemnity is a promise to cover the other party's losses from specified third-party claims, most often intellectual-property infringement, breach of law, and bodily injury or property damage.
entries.standard_position: Vendor indemnifies for third-party IP infringement claims, violation of law and gross negligence, with customer control of settlement consent; customer indemnity limited to misuse of the services.
fallbacks: Accept vendor's right to control defence if customer keeps settlement veto for admissions of fault
Accept exclusion of claims arising from customer-provided data or modifications

precedents.text: Vendor deleted the IP indemnity entirely. Restored with a remedy ladder (procure the right, modify, replace, refund).
Vendor required customer to indemnify for all claims related to use of the services. Narrowed to claims from customer data and breach of acceptable-use terms.

entries.definition: Intellectual-property ownership clauses decide who owns deliverables, work product, customer data and any improvements the vendor makes during the engagement.
entries.standard_position: Customer owns deliverables and all customer data; vendor retains pre-existing IP and tools with a perpetual licence to customer for anything embedded in deliverables; no vendor rights in customer data beyond providing the service.
fallbacks: Vendor keeps generic know-how and reusable components not specific to customer
Joint ownership of jointly developed improvements with mutual licence

precedents.text: Vendor's terms kept all deliverables as vendor property with a term-limited licence. Rejected as a deal-breaker for bespoke work; vendor accepted customer ownership of custom deliverables.
Vendor claimed rights to use customer data to train models. Struck; replaced with aggregated, de-identified usage statistics only.

entries.definition: Termination clauses set who may end the agreement, on what notice, for convenience or for cause, and what cure period and transition assistance apply.
entries.standard_position: Either party may terminate for uncured material breach on 30 days' written notice; customer may terminate for convenience on 60 days' notice with pro-rata refund of prepaid fees; 90 days of transition assistance at then-current rates.
fallbacks: Convenience termination after an initial 12-month commitment
Early-termination fee capped at 3 months of fees

precedents.text: Vendor allowed termination for convenience by vendor only, on 10 days' notice. Made mutual at 60 days with transition assistance.
Vendor removed the cure period for customer breach. Restored 30-day cure for non-payment and other breaches.

entries.definition: Governing-law and venue clauses choose which jurisdiction's law interprets the contract and where disputes are heard.
entries.standard_position: Laws of the State of New York, exclusive venue in New York courts, waiver of jury trial; no foreign law for a US counterparty.
fallbacks: Delaware law with Delaware venue
Neutral US jurisdiction where vendor is not incorporated if vendor insists on home state

precedents.text: Vendor proposed the law of its home state (California) with venue in San Francisco. Settled on Delaware as neutral.
Foreign vendor proposed English law and London courts. Rejected for a US-only deployment; accepted New York with English-language proceedings.

entries.definition: Dispute-resolution clauses decide whether disputes go to court or binding arbitration, under which rules, and whether class actions are waived.
entries.standard_position: Escalation to executives for 30 days, then litigation in the agreed venue; no mandatory arbitration; injunctive relief available for IP and confidentiality breaches.
fallbacks: Arbitration under AAA commercial rules with a single arbitrator for claims under $250,000
Mediation before litigation

precedents.text: Vendor required binding arbitration in its home city with a class-action waiver. Countered with executive escalation then courts; vendor accepted mediation-first.

entries.definition: Payment terms fix invoice timing, due dates, late fees, disputed-invoice handling and currency.
entries.standard_position: Net 45 from receipt of a correct invoice; disputed amounts withheld in good faith without penalty; late interest capped at 1% per month; annual increases capped at CPI or 3%.
fallbacks: Net 30 in exchange for a 2% early-payment discount
Late interest at 1.5% per month after a 15-day grace period

precedents.text: Vendor proposed net 15 with 2% monthly late fees and suspension rights after 5 days. Settled at net 30, 1% late fee, 30-day suspension notice.
Vendor proposed annual price increases at vendor's discretion. Capped at the greater of CPI or 3%.

entries.definition: Penalty and service-credit clauses set the financial consequences of missed service levels or late delivery.
entries.standard_position: Service credits of 5-25% of monthly fees by severity of SLA miss, credits are not the exclusive remedy for chronic failure; no penalties on customer beyond late-payment interest.
fallbacks: Credits as exclusive remedy below three consecutive misses, termination right above
Credit cap at 50% of monthly fees

precedents.text: Vendor set credits as the sole and exclusive remedy for any SLA failure. Added a termination right after three misses in six months.

entries.definition: Breach clauses define what counts as material breach, the cure period, and the remedies available beyond termination.
entries.standard_position: Material breach defined with examples; 30-day cure period; remedies cumulative; suspension only for non-payment after notice or security emergencies.
fallbacks: 10-day cure for non-payment, 30 days for other breaches
Immediate suspension for verified security threats with notice within 24 hours

precedents.text: Vendor could suspend services immediately for any alleged breach. Narrowed to non-payment after notice and genuine security emergencies.

entries.definition: Confidentiality clauses define protected information, permitted disclosures, the standard of care, and how long obligations survive.
entries.standard_position: Mutual; obligations survive 5 years after termination, indefinitely for trade secrets and personal data; disclosure permitted to advisers under equivalent obligations and when compelled by law with notice.
fallbacks: 3-year survival for general confidential information with indefinite survival for trade secrets
Residual-knowledge clause limited to unaided memory and excluding customer data

precedents.text: Vendor's survival period was 1 year. Extended to 3 years plus indefinite for trade secrets and personal data.
Vendor included a broad residuals clause. Accepted only with an exclusion for customer data and source code.

entries.definition: Exclusivity and non-compete clauses restrict one party from buying from, selling to, or working with competitors.
entries.standard_position: No exclusivity; no restriction on customer using competing services; no non-solicit of customer employees beyond a mutual 12-month, named-employee restriction.
fallbacks: Preferred-vendor status without exclusivity
Right of first refusal on additional scope with a 15-day response window

precedents.text: Vendor asked for exclusivity in the customer's product category for 3 years. Rejected; offered a non-binding preferred-vendor letter.

entries.definition: Auto-renewal clauses extend the term automatically unless a party gives notice of non-renewal within a window before expiry.
entries.standard_position: Renewal only by written agreement; if auto-renewal is accepted, 12-month terms with a 60-day non-renewal window and vendor reminder notice 90 days before expiry.
fallbacks: Auto-renewal with a 30-day window and price cap on the renewal term
Month-to-month after the initial term

precedents.text: Vendor's terms auto-renewed for 3-year periods with a 180-day notice window. Reduced to 12-month renewals, 60-day window, reminder notice required.

entries.definition: Warranties are promises about the quality of services or deliverables, their conformance to documentation, and non-infringement; disclaimers limit implied warranties.
entries.standard_position: Services perform materially per documentation; deliverables free of malicious code; professional and workmanlike performance; disclaimer of implied warranties accepted only if the express warranties above remain.
fallbacks: 90-day warranty period on deliverables with re-performance as the remedy
Accept 'as is' only for beta features clearly labelled as such

precedents.text: Vendor disclaimed all warranties including conformance to documentation. Restored the documentation warranty with re-performance or refund as remedy.

entries.definition: Notice clauses fix how and when formal notices are given and how much advance notice changes, terminations or renewals require.
entries.standard_position: Written notice by email with confirmation or courier; 30 days' notice for scope changes; notices effective on receipt.
fallbacks: Accept 35-45 days for change notices
Email-only notice to named contacts with read receipt

precedents.text: Vendor required 35 days' notice for changes against our 30. Accepted; the 5-day gap had no operational impact.

entries.definition: Amendment clauses set how the contract may be changed, typically only in a signed writing, and whether online terms can be updated unilaterally.
entries.standard_position: Amendments only by written agreement signed by both parties; no unilateral updates to incorporated online terms that reduce customer rights.
fallbacks: Vendor may update online policies with 30 days' notice and customer termination right if materially adverse

precedents.text: Vendor's terms allowed updates to policies at any time by posting. Added notice plus termination right for adverse changes.

entries.definition: Assignment clauses control whether a party may transfer the contract to another entity, including in a merger or sale.
entries.standard_position: No assignment without consent, not unreasonably withheld, except to an affiliate or successor in a merger or asset sale with notice.
fallbacks: Consent not required for assignment to a non-competitor successor
Assignment permitted with 30 days' notice and a termination right for the other party

precedents.text: Vendor could assign freely while customer needed consent. Made mutual with the merger carve-out.

entries.definition: Subcontracting clauses govern whether the vendor may delegate performance and who is responsible for subcontractor acts.
entries.standard_position: Subcontracting permitted with notice; vendor remains fully liable for subcontractors; subcontractors bound by equivalent confidentiality and security terms; customer may object to subprocessors of personal data.
fallbacks: Pre-approved subcontractor list in an exhibit, additions on 30 days' notice

precedents.text: Vendor's terms disclaimed liability for subcontractor performance. Restored full vendor responsibility.

entries.definition: Insurance clauses require minimum coverage types and limits (general liability, cyber, errors and omissions) and proof of coverage.
entries.standard_position: Vendor maintains general liability $2M per occurrence, cyber and E&O $5M aggregate, workers' compensation as required by law; certificates on request; subcontractors covered to the same level.
fallbacks: Cyber/E&O $2M for engagements under $500K annual value

precedents.text: Vendor offered $1M general liability and no cyber cover. Settled at $2M GL and $3M cyber given data access.

entries.definition: Force majeure clauses excuse performance during events beyond a party's reasonable control and set notice, mitigation and termination rights for prolonged events.
entries.standard_position: Mutual; excludes payment obligations and events the affected party could have mitigated (including ordinary labour disputes and supplier failures); termination right after 60 days of continuous excuse.
fallbacks: 90-day termination trigger
Pandemic and cyber-attack listed expressly with a business-continuity obligation

precedents.text: Vendor's clause excused vendor only and included 'supplier failure' broadly. Made mutual, narrowed supplier failure to events beyond the supplier's control.

entries.definition: A clause open to more than one reasonable reading, where the difference between the two contracts is about wording rather than obligation.
entries.standard_position: Flag as LOW with the two readings stated; request clarifying language rather than a substantive change.
fallbacks: Add a definition to the definitions section
Add an interpretive sentence rather than rewriting the clause

precedents.text: 'Business day' undefined in vendor terms. Added a definition; no substantive negotiation required.

entries.definition: A difference in numbering, cross-references, defined terms or formatting that does not change either party's obligations.
entries.standard_position: Note it, propose a conforming edit, do not negotiate.
fallbacks: Fix in the final conformed copy

precedents.text: Vendor referred to 'Section 11' for insurance where the company's document used 'Section 10'. Conformed in the final copy.

entries.definition: Data-protection clauses govern processing of personal data, security standards, breach notification and subprocessor rules, often through a data processing addendum.
entries.standard_position: DPA incorporated; vendor as processor; breach notification within 48 hours; SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001; deletion or return of data within 30 days of termination.
fallbacks: 72-hour breach notification
Annual penetration test summary in lieu of full audit rights

precedents.text: Vendor offered breach notification 'without undue delay' with no deadline. Fixed at 72 hours.

entries.definition: Service-level clauses set uptime, response and resolution targets and how they are measured and reported.
entries.standard_position: 99.9% monthly uptime measured across all regions; P1 response 1 hour, resolution target 4 hours; monthly SLA report; credits per the penalties entry.
fallbacks: 99.5% uptime for non-production environments
Exclusion of scheduled maintenance capped at 8 hours per month with 5 days' notice

precedents.text: Vendor's uptime target was 99% with unlimited scheduled maintenance. Settled at 99.9% with a maintenance cap.

entries.definition: Audit clauses let one party verify the other's compliance with security, financial or licence terms, subject to notice and frequency limits.
entries.standard_position: Annual audit right on 30 days' notice, plus after any security incident; third-party audit reports accepted in lieu where available.
fallbacks: Audit at customer's cost unless material non-compliance is found

precedents.text: Vendor refused any audit right. Accepted SOC 2 report delivery annually plus incident-triggered audits.
